segments.english: Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn, and Heth.
segments.literal: and-Canaan begot [object-marker] Sidon his-firstborn and-[object-marker] Heth

tokens.note: qatal; with a male subject yalad means 'beget'
construct form of bekhor with the suffix -o 'his'

phrases.literal: 'and-Canaan begot'; the waw only continues the list of Ham's sons

grammar: The verb יָלַד, with a man as subject, means 'beget'; the objects are marked by אֶת.
בְּכֹרוֹ stands in apposition to צִידֹן and is set off by the tipḥa.
The waw on וּכְנַעַן is a simple connective with the preceding sons of Ham.
segments.note: The ancestor-name Canaan is also the ethnic name; the English keeps the name. Ramban's discussion of how the ten peoples relate to the land promised to Abraham is a historical comment, not about the words.

commentary.summary: Ramban: these are the ten peoples of Canaan given to Abraham; their names changed over time. This concerns the identification of the peoples, not the plain sense of the clause.
Radak finds no clear reason for בְּכֹרוֹ here; he suggests Sidon is named for both rank and birth order. The English simply says 'his firstborn'.

apparatus: Onkelos: וּכְנַעַן אוֹלִיד יָת צִידוֹן בָּכְרֵיהּ וְיָת חֵת, in agreement with the Hebrew.

segments.english: the Jebusites, the Amorites, and the Girgashites.
segments.literal: and-[object-marker] the-Jebusite and-[object-marker] the-Amorite and-[object-marker] the-Girgashite

phrases.literal: 'and-[object-marker] the-Girgashite'; English places 'and' before the last item

grammar: Each name is a gentilic in the singular with the article, used for the whole people, and each is the object of the verb in 10:15.
The disjunctive accents pashta and zaqef qaton divide the list into three.
segments.note: The English puts 'and' only before the last item, as English lists do; the literal line keeps every waw.

commentary.summary: Radak: all these names have the gentilic ending and the article because they name the peoples descended from them, not an individual.

apparatus: Onkelos renders the gentilics with the Aramaic ending -אֵי.

segments.english: the Hivites, the Arkites, and the Sinites.
segments.literal: and-[object-marker] the-Hivite and-[object-marker] the-Arkite and-[object-marker] the-Sinite
grammar: The list continues as objects of יָלַד in 10:15, each introduced by אֶת.
The definite article after the object marker shows that these are names of peoples.
segments.note: The lexicon glosses חִוִּי as 'villagers'; the English uses the ethnic name Hivites.
apparatus: Onkelos: וְיָת אַנְתּוֹסָאֵי for the Sinites.

segments.english: the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites spread out.
segments.literal: and-[object-marker] the-Arvadite and-[object-marker] the-Zemarite and-[object-marker] the-Hamathite and-afterward were-scattered clans-of the-Canaanite

tokens.note: adverb after waw; the etnaḥta before it ends the list
Niphal qatal, 'were scattered'; middle sense 'spread out'

phrases.literal: 'and-afterward'; the waw only joins the sentence to the list

phrases.english: the clans of the Canaanites spread out
phrases.literal: 'were-scattered clans-of the-Canaanite'; verb first, subject after; English puts the subject first

grammar: The etnaḥta on הַחֲמָתִי ends the list of Canaan's sons; a new sentence begins with וְאַחַר.
נָפֹצוּ is Niphal qatal of פוץ, 'were scattered' (in the sense of spreading out); the subject מִשְׁפְּחוֹת follows the verb.
Word order here is verb, then subject.
segments.note: The 'afterward' is read, with Radak, as after the dispersion at Babel (the pelagah); Rashi does not specify the time, only that many clans spread from these peoples. The English does not decide the time.

commentary.summary: Rashi: from these peoples many clans were scattered. The English takes the subject as the clans of the Canaanites spreading out.
Radak: 'afterward' means after the division (the Babel dispersion).

apparatus: Onkelos: וּבָתַר כֵּן אִתְבַּדָּרוּ זַרְעֲיַת כְּנַעֲנָאֵי, 'and after that the families of the Canaanites were dispersed'.

segments.english: The border of the Canaanites ran from Sidon toward Gerar, as far as Gaza; toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.
segments.literal: and-was border-of the-Canaanite from-Sidon as-you-come Gerar-ward as-far-as Gaza as-you-come Sodom-ward and-Gomorrah and-Admah and-Zeboiim as-far-as Lasha

tokens.note: infinitive construct with 2nd person masculine singular suffix, 'your coming'

phrases.english: The border of the Canaanites ran
phrases.literal: 'and-was border-of the-Canaanite'; the border 'was' from Sidon to ...
'as-you-come Gerar-ward'; the idiom, read with Ibn Ezra as 'to Gerar'

grammar: בֹּאֲכָה is an infinitive construct of בוא with a 2nd person suffix, 'your coming'; it works as an idiom 'in the direction of'.
The directional he on גְרָרָה and סְדֹמָה means 'to Gerar', 'to Sodom'.
The gershayim and zaqef qaton mark the main divisions: Sidon, then Gaza, then the Sodom group and Lasha.
Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim are listed with waw between the last three.
segments.note: בֹּאֲכָה is read with Ibn Ezra as 'toward' (אל גרר); Rashi's alternative, a speaker telling a friend that the border reaches 'until you come to' a given place, is recorded. The English 'toward' fits both. The border was drawn on the line given, going from Sidon in the north to Lasha; the sequence of places is not further identified here.

commentary.summary: Rashi: גְּבוּל means the end of his land; every גְּבוּל means end and edge. The English 'border' follows this.
Rashi: בֹּאֲכָה is a noun in his view, and to him it is like a man telling a friend that the border runs until you come to such a place. The English uses 'toward', which does not contradict it.
Ibn Ezra: בֹּאֲכָה גְרָרָה means 'to Gerar'. The English 'toward Gerar' follows.
Radak: the passage shows that God intended the Canaanites to settle the land until their end, for Israel's sake. This is theological, not about the words.

apparatus: Onkelos: וַהֲוָה תְּחוּם כְּנַעֲנָאֵי מִצִּידוֹן מָטֵי לִגְרָר עַד עַזָּה, 'reaching to Gerar'.
Lasha is not identified with any known place in the pack.

segments.english: These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, by their languages, in their lands, in their nations.
segments.literal: these sons-of Ham to-their-clans to-their-tongues in-their-lands in-their-nations

phrases.english: These are the sons of Ham

grammar: A nominal clause: אֵלֶּה is the subject, בְנֵי־חָם the predicate.
The four phrases with ל and ב give the divisions of Ham's descendants.
The paragraph mark (ס) closes the section on the sons of Ham.
segments.note: The prepositions ל and ב are rendered 'by' and 'in' for a smooth English line.

commentary.summary: Rashi: though they were divided into languages and lands, all of them are sons of Ham.
Ibn Ezra: the same formula is said of the sons of Japheth and the sons of Shem.

apparatus: Onkelos: אִלֵּין בְּנֵי חָם לְזַרְעֲיָתְהוֹן לְלִישָׁנְהוֹן בְּאַרְעָתְהוֹן בְּעַמְמֵיהוֹן.
